• Skin moisturization and protection
• Beauty traditional uses
products.processing_method:
• Cluster Harvesting: Only wild-grown palm clusters from mature Elaeis oleifera trees are collected.
• Fruit Removal: Individual ripe fruits are manually detached from clusters and gathered in woven baskets.
• Boiling: Fruits are boiled in clean water over controlled wood fires until adequate steam release indicates readiness.
• Pulp Removal: Softened fruits are crushed in wooden mortars (pilón) to separate pulp and shells from kernels.
• Sun-Drying: Kernels are sun-dried for 4–8 days, turned regularly for uniform moisture reduction.
• Heat Extraction: Dried kernels are crushed and heated over controlled fires to gradually release the oil.
• Filtration: Hot oil is strained through clean cotton cloth, then cooled gradually. No chemical filters are used.
• Packing & Export: Oil is bottled in sterile containers and prepared to meet international export standards.

products.processing_method:
• Sustainable Harvesting: Local harvesters use hand-picking techniques to collect herbs from various regions and forests in Honduras. This step requires intimate knowledge of the flora to ensure only the correct species are harvested at their peak, often in the early morning after dew has dried. It also ensures that only a small portion of any plant population is gathered, protecting local ecosystems.
• Initial Sorting and Garbling: As the herbs are picked, unwanted debris such as dirt, dead leaves, and other plant matter is removed by hand. The herbs are then sorted by type, and for some preparations, major stems and tougher parts are separated from more delicate leaves and flowers.
• Bundling or Spreading for Drying: For delicate herbs with stems (like those harvested for leaves and flowers), they are often tied into small, loose bunches and hung upside down. For roots, bark, or loose leaves, they are spread in a single, thin layer on ventilated drying beds. This method ensures maximum airflow around each piece of plant material.
• Natural Shade Drying: The beds and bundles are placed in a cool, dry, and well-ventilated area that is protected from direct sunlight, wind, and pests. This slow, indirect drying process prevents the degradation of heat-sensitive volatile oils, preserving the herbs' aroma, color, and therapeutic properties.
• Final Processing and Storage: Once the herbs are completely dry and brittle, they are removed from their bundles. Any remaining stems or undesirable parts are garbled out. The herbs are then stored in airtight containers, away from light and moisture, to maintain their potency and extend their shelf life. For teas, leaves are often left whole until use to preserve their essential oils.
